title: Position, path and the reference frame
subtitle: Kinematics begins by saying where, when, and relative to what.
takeaway: Choose origin, axis, and clock first; displacement is final minus initial position, while distance counts the whole path.

cards.title: A coordinate is not the motion
items: A 1-D frame is an origin, a positive direction, and a clock. Position $x(t)$ is measured from that origin. Changing origin changes coordinates, not the physical path.
Write the sign convention before equations. “Left” is not automatically negative; it is negative only if left is chosen as the negative axis.

cards.title: Displacement is an endpoint difference
items: From $x_i$ to $x_f$, displacement is signed. A round trip has zero displacement even though motion occurred. Displacement depends only on endpoints, not the route.
Move from 2 m to 7 m, then to 4 m: net displacement is +2 m.

cards.title: Distance is accumulated path length
items: Distance never decreases and never carries a direction. It adds every segment, including retracing. For a differentiable path, add the magnitude of each small displacement.
Do not replace distance by $|x_f-x_i|$ after a reversal; that misses the path already travelled.

cards.title: A quick counterexample
items: A walker goes east 5 m and west 3 m. The final point is 2 m east of the start, but the route length is 8 m. The ratio $|\Delta x|/d$ lies from 0 to 1.
Equality $d=|\Delta x|$ holds only when direction never reverses.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Average and instantaneous velocity
subtitle: Velocity is the signed rate of position change; speed is its magnitude.
takeaway: A secant slope gives average velocity; a tangent slope gives instantaneous velocity.

cards.title: Average velocity uses net change
items: Over a time interval, average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time. It can be positive, negative, or zero; it is not average speed.
A round trip has zero average velocity because its net displacement is zero, even though its average speed is positive.

cards.title: Instantaneous velocity is a limit
items: Shrink the interval around the instant. The limiting secant slope becomes the tangent slope of $x$ versus $t$. A positive or negative sign identifies direction on the chosen axis.

cards.title: Speed forgets direction
items: Speed is the non-negative magnitude of velocity. Average speed uses total distance, so it is at least the magnitude of average velocity.
Do not average signed velocities and call the result average speed.

cards.title: Relative position changes the frame
items: For two objects measured in the same frame, define $x_{AB}=x_A-x_B$. Its derivative is the velocity of A as seen from B. This definition fixes the subtraction order.
If A moves at 8 m/s right and B at 3 m/s right, A gains on B at 5 m/s.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Acceleration and the meaning of signs
subtitle: Acceleration measures velocity change, not “slowing down.”
takeaway: Same signs of v and a increase speed; opposite signs decrease speed.

cards.title: Average and instantaneous acceleration
items: Acceleration is the rate of velocity change. It may be positive, negative, or zero; the sign describes direction of velocity change, not whether the object is speeding up.
A car can move right while acceleration points left: it is moving right but losing speed.

cards.title: Use the sign product
items: For one-dimensional motion at nonzero speed, the rate of change of speed has the sign of $v a$. Thus speed increases when $va>0$ and decreases when $va<0$.
At a turning point $v=0$, inspect the motion on each side; the sign test is not defined at that instant.

cards.title: Four sign combinations
items: Rightward motion with rightward acceleration speeds up; rightward with leftward acceleration slows. Leftward with leftward acceleration speeds up left; leftward with rightward acceleration slows.
“Negative acceleration” is not a synonym for deceleration. The axis orientation may be reversed.

cards.title: Dimensions expose mistakes
items: Velocity has dimensions length/time; acceleration has length/time squared. A slope on an x-t graph has velocity units; a slope on a v-t graph has acceleration units.
A claimed acceleration in m/s is missing one factor of time in the denominator.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Position, velocity and acceleration graphs
subtitle: A graph is a calculator: slopes differentiate and signed areas integrate.
takeaway: x-t slope is v; v-t slope is a and signed area is displacement; a-t area is change in v.

cards.title: Read x versus t
items: The slope of a chord is average velocity; the tangent slope is instantaneous velocity. A horizontal tangent means $v=0$ at that instant, not necessarily that the particle stays at rest.
A curved x-t graph still describes one-dimensional motion; the curve is not the path through space.

cards.title: Read v versus t
items: Slope gives acceleration. Signed area from $t_1$ to $t_2$ gives displacement. To get distance, split at every zero of v and add the absolute areas.
If v changes sign, net displacement can be small while total distance is large.

cards.title: Read a versus t
items: The signed area under acceleration gives change in velocity. Add the initial velocity to recover $v(t)$. Acceleration alone does not give position until you integrate again and supply initial data.
The integration constants are physical initial conditions, not optional algebra.

cards.title: Cross-check slopes and areas
items: If a is constant, v-t is a straight line and x-t is a parabola. If v is constant, x-t is a straight line and a-t is zero. Use these shape relations to catch sign errors.
A positive triangular area below the t-axis is negative displacement, not negative distance.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Constant-acceleration equations
subtitle: Derive the familiar equations from integration; use them only when a is constant.
takeaway: Every constant-a formula comes from the straight-line v-t graph; time-free form follows by elimination.

cards.title: Velocity after time t
items: For constant acceleration, integrate $dv/dt=a$ and apply $v(0)=u$. The result is linear in time. The sign of a is retained. If v and a share a sign, speed grows; if their signs oppose, speed falls until a turning point.

cards.title: Displacement from the v-t area
items: The signed trapezoid under a straight v-t line has area average endpoint velocity times time. This gives displacement, including cases where one endpoint velocity is negative; if a reversal lies inside, signed area still works.
The trapezoid form uses endpoint velocities; the polynomial form uses initial velocity and acceleration.

cards.title: Eliminate time
items: From $v-u=at$, substitute into displacement or use $a=v\,dv/dx$ with constant a. The resulting relation does not require time, but still assumes constant acceleration.
A position-dependent or speed-dependent acceleration invalidates this equation unless a is constant over the interval.

cards.title: Choose the equation by the missing variable
items: Known $u,a,t$: find v or displacement. Known $u,v,t$: use the trapezoid. Known $u,v,a$: eliminate t. Set a clear signed coordinate before substitution.
Every term in an equation for displacement must have units of length.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Free fall and vertical throws
subtitle: Near Earth, gravity is approximately constant and points downward.
takeaway: Choose up positive: a = -g at every point, including the apex.

cards.title: Choose the axis once
items: With upward positive and negligible air resistance, acceleration is $-g$. Use the same convention for initial velocity, displacement, and final velocity; do not switch signs mid-solution.
At the top, v is momentarily zero but gravity still accelerates the ball downward.

cards.title: Rise from launch level
items: For initial upward speed $u>0$, the apex occurs when $v=0$. The rise and ascent time follow from constant-a kinematics.
If u doubles, the maximum rise becomes four times as large.

cards.title: Return to the launch elevation
items: In vacuum, motion is symmetric about the apex for equal start/end elevations. The total time is twice the ascent time; the return velocity has the same magnitude and opposite sign.
This symmetry fails with drag or when comparing unequal elevations.

cards.title: General vertical position equation
items: For launch position $y_0$ and signed initial velocity $u$, solve $y-y_0=ut-gt^2/2$. A height can be crossed twice; retain non-negative roots and interpret direction from v.
For a drop from rest through height h: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$ and impact speed $\sqrt{2gh}$.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Displacement during the nth second
subtitle: An interval formula gives signed displacement, not automatically distance.
takeaway: Subtract x(n) - x(n-1); if velocity reverses within the interval, split and take absolute areas.

cards.title: Derive by subtraction
items: For constant a, write $x(t)-x(0)=ut+at^2/2$. Subtract the displacement at $n-1$ seconds from that at n seconds.
Here n counts one-second intervals. For intervals of duration delta, subtract x(ndelta)-x((n-1)delta) instead.

cards.title: Signed interval result
items: The expression can be negative if the particle moves left overall during that second. It is the area under v-t between n-1 and n seconds.
With u=0, a=4 m/s², the third-second displacement is 10 m.

cards.title: When is it a distance?
items: If v keeps one sign throughout the interval, distance is $|\Delta x_n|$. If v crosses zero, split at $t_*=-u/a$ and add the magnitudes of the two signed pieces.
Do not call a negative nth-second displacement a negative distance.

cards.title: A reversal example
items: Let $u=2$ m/s and $a=-4$ m/s². The turn occurs at 0.5 s. During the first second the signed displacement is zero, but the particle travels 0.5 m out and 0.5 m back.
This is why distance must be found by absolute velocity area.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Variable acceleration: integrate with initial data
subtitle: If a changes, return to definitions instead of using constant-a formulas.
takeaway: Given a(t), integrate twice; use initial velocity and position to determine both constants.

cards.title: Acceleration given as a(t)
items: Integrate acceleration to obtain velocity, then integrate velocity to obtain position. At each stage insert the corresponding initial condition.

cards.title: Acceleration given as a(v)
items: Use $dv/dt=a(v)$ to separate variables and find elapsed time as a function of velocity. The integral must respect the initial and final velocities and any singular points.
This route can reveal terminal speed as an equilibrium where a(v)=0.

cards.title: Acceleration given as a(x)
items: Chain rule gives $dv/dt=(dv/dx)(dx/dt)=v\,dv/dx$. It converts acceleration-versus-position into an integral for v squared.
The result fixes v²; choose the velocity sign on each branch and split at a turning point.

cards.title: The method must match the given variable
items: Use t when a is specified in time, v when it is specified in speed, x when position dependence is explicit. If acceleration depends on multiple variables, solve the actual differential equation or use a justified substitution.
Initial conditions are required to recover the physical trajectory.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: The v dv/dx method and turning points
subtitle: The chain rule converts a second-order time law into an energy-like position relation.
takeaway: Integrate v dv = a(x) dx, keep the integration constant, then check where v² can remain non-negative.

cards.title: Derive the identity
items: For a differentiable trajectory, apply the chain rule to v as a function of x along the motion. This does not require constant acceleration.
This is especially useful when acceleration depends on position but time is absent.

cards.title: Example: restoring acceleration
items: Suppose $a=-kx$ with k positive and initial state x=0, v=v0. Integrate from 0 to x. The accessible positions satisfy v squared non-negative.
Turning points occur at $x=\pm v_0/\sqrt{k}$. The result describes bounded motion.

cards.title: Sign branches matter
items: The equation gives $v=\pm\sqrt{v_0^2-kx^2}$. Choose the sign from the direction of travel; after a turning point the sign changes while the same v² relation can still hold.
Do not take the positive square root for both the outward and return branches.

cards.title: Check the dimensions and limit
items: For $a=-kx$, k has units s^-2. Then $v_0^2/k$ has units m². As k tends to zero, the turning point recedes without bound, consistent with vanishing restoring acceleration.
At x=0, the formula returns the initial speed magnitude $v_0$.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Relative motion on a line
subtitle: Subtract velocities in one shared frame; use signed separation to decide approach.
takeaway: v_AB = v_A - v_B. The sign of relative velocity alone is not the closing direction; check separation too.

cards.title: Define relative position first
items: Set $r=x_A-x_B$. Then $dr/dt=v_A-v_B$. If r is positive, A is to the right; the gap shrinks when r and dr/dt have opposite signs.
A at x=10 moving left at 2, B at x=0 moving right at 1: r>0 and v_AB=-3, so they approach.

cards.title: Closing speed is a magnitude
items: Closing speed is $-|dr/dt|$ only when the pair is approaching; its positive magnitude is $|v_A-v_B|$. Equal direction speeds subtract; opposite directions add.
Relative velocity is signed. “Closing speed” is non-negative and only meaningful while the gap decreases.

cards.title: Constant relative acceleration
items: When both accelerations are constant, relative position obeys the same kinematic equations with $a_{AB}=a_A-a_B$. This can reduce two trajectories to one gap equation.
A catch or meeting is a root of r(t)=0; check the root is in the physical time interval.

cards.title: Worked catch-up check
items: A leads by 100 m. A moves at 10 m/s, B follows at 15 m/s. The gap closes at 5 m/s, so catch-up takes 20 s; both positions then agree.
For two trains approaching at 80 and 60 km/h, closing speed is 140 km/h, not 20 km/h.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Piecewise motion and stopping distance
subtitle: Break a motion at every change in acceleration or constraint; match state between phases.
takeaway: Position and velocity carry across a smooth phase boundary; braking distance scales as speed squared.

cards.title: Build a state ledger
items: For each phase record start time, duration, initial x and v, acceleration, final x and v. A phase ends with the next phase’s initial state unless an impact or impulse changes velocity.
The ledger prevents accidental resets of position or velocity when a changes.

cards.title: Brake under constant deceleration
items: For initial speed u and deceleration magnitude b, set signed acceleration opposite the motion. Solve $0=u^2-2b d$ for stopping distance, or $0=u-bt$ for stopping time.
Doubling u doubles stopping time but quadruples braking distance if b is unchanged.

cards.title: Reaction distance is separate
items: During a reaction delay $t_r$, the driver has not yet braked; at unchanged speed the extra distance is $u t_r$. Total stopping distance is reaction distance plus braking distance.
Do not call the braking distance the total stopping distance when reaction time is supplied.

cards.title: Piecewise graph audit
items: On a v-t graph, each phase is a segment. Add signed areas for total displacement; add absolute areas after splitting at every zero of v for distance.
If a phase starts with negative velocity, positive acceleration may first reduce speed before reversing direction.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Projectile motion starts with components
subtitle: Resolve launch velocity; gravity changes only the vertical component in the vacuum model.
takeaway: Horizontal and vertical equations share time t; their only coupling is the common clock.

cards.title: Choose axes and initial components
items: Take x horizontal and y upward. A launch speed v0 at angle theta above horizontal has components found by projection onto the axes.
At theta=0 the launch is horizontal; at theta=90 degrees it is vertical.

cards.title: Independent accelerations
items: Neglecting drag, the only acceleration is gravity. Horizontal velocity is constant; vertical velocity decreases linearly.
A horizontal launch and a vertical drop from the same height have identical vertical motion.

cards.title: Parametric trajectory
items: With launch point at the origin, integrate each component. The equations hold until the projectile hits a surface or the assumptions fail.
The path in space is not the x-t graph. x(t) and y(t) are coordinates at the same time.

cards.title: Independence test
items: At any fixed time, vertical drop is $gt^2/2$, independent of horizontal launch speed. In the same ideal conditions, horizontal and dropped balls hit together.
Changing horizontal speed changes where the ball lands, not when it reaches a given vertical level.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Horizontal launch from a height
subtitle: The vertical fall determines flight time; horizontal speed sets range.
takeaway: For a level ground h below launch: t = sqrt(2h/g), R = v0 sqrt(2h/g).

cards.title: Solve time from vertical motion
items: A horizontal launch has initial vertical velocity zero. With the ground h below the launch point, solve the vertical displacement equation for the positive flight time.
Time is independent of horizontal speed in the no-drag model.

cards.title: Find horizontal range
items: Horizontal acceleration is zero, so the range from the cliff edge is constant horizontal speed times flight time. A vertical launch has zero range but still takes finite time to fall from a nonzero height.
The equation assumes a level landing surface at height h below launch.

cards.title: Impact velocity and speed
items: At impact, horizontal velocity remains v0 and vertical velocity is downward with magnitude gt. Use vector components for direction and Pythagoras for speed.
Impact speed is not the horizontal speed; gravity has added vertical kinetic motion.

cards.title: Worked scale check
items: For v0=15 m/s, h=20 m, g=10 m/s², flight time is 2 s and range is 30 m. The vertical impact speed is 20 m/s.
The 25 m/s impact speed follows from sqrt(15²+20²), a useful independent check. The 30 m range is horizontal displacement only; the actual curved path is longer.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Oblique launch: time, height and range
subtitle: For launch and landing at equal elevations, solve y(T)=0 for the nonzero root.
takeaway: T = 2v0 sintheta/g, H = v0² sin²theta/(2g), R = v0² sin2theta/g under equal-height vacuum conditions.

cards.title: Time to return to launch elevation
items: Set vertical displacement to zero. The root t=0 is launch; the second root is the return time. It is positive for an upward launch; a horizontal launch from the same level has no later return.
This is not the flight time to a cliff floor or a higher platform.

cards.title: Maximum height
items: At the apex the vertical component vanishes. Apply the vertical constant-a equation to obtain height above launch point. At fixed launch speed, a larger vertical component raises the apex but leaves less speed for horizontal motion.
Only vertical launch speed contributes to the height.

cards.title: Horizontal range
items: The horizontal component is constant. Multiply it by flight time and use the double-angle identity. The result is a signed x displacement; if the chosen launch direction points backward, keep the negative sign.
Range is maximized at 45 degrees only when launch and landing elevations match and speed is fixed.

cards.title: Useful elimination
items: For the equal-height case, combine range and height to relate trajectory shape without v0 or g. At 30 degrees, R/H is 4 times sqrt(3); the ratio compares horizontal reach with peak rise.
At a vertical launch, R=0; at 45 degrees, R is maximum.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Trajectory, velocity and speed at a height
subtitle: Eliminate time for the path; retain components for velocity and angle.
takeaway: The vacuum trajectory is a downward-opening parabola; at a given height the speed is launch speed adjusted by vertical rise.

cards.title: Eliminate time to get y(x)
items: From x=v0 costheta t, solve for t and substitute into y(t). This assumes costheta is nonzero; vertical launch is a separate straight-line limit.
The quadratic coefficient is negative for g>0, so the path curves downward.

cards.title: Velocity direction along the path
items: Horizontal velocity stays fixed; vertical velocity changes with time. The flight-path angle phi satisfies tanphi=vy/vx whenever vx is nonzero.
At the apex phi=0; the velocity is horizontal, not zero unless the launch was vertical.

cards.title: Speed at vertical rise y
items: With gravity only, $v_x^2+v_y^2=v_0^2-2gy$ for launch from y=0. It is an energy-like kinematic identity; it does not determine direction by itself.
If y exceeds v0²/(2g), the right side is negative: that height is unreachable.

cards.title: Same height, same speed
items: For a vacuum projectile, at any later point at the launch elevation the speed magnitude returns to v0. At a different height, vertical speed magnitude is fixed by the equation above.
For ground-to-ground flight, the landing angle is -theta and the landing speed equals launch speed.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Range twins and the maximum range
subtitle: The sine of twice the angle creates complementary-angle symmetry.
takeaway: Angles theta and 90°-theta give the same range, but not the same height or flight time.

cards.title: Complementary angles are range twins
items: For equal launch and landing elevations, R depends on sin 2theta. Replacing theta by 90°-theta leaves this sine unchanged.
A 30-degree shot and a 60-degree shot have equal range at the same speed.

cards.title: But their arcs differ
items: The steeper shot has larger vertical component, so it reaches greater height and stays in flight longer, while the horizontal component is smaller.
Equal range does not imply equal trajectory, impact time, or impact velocity vector.

cards.title: Maximum range condition
items: At fixed v0 and g, maximize sin 2theta over 0 to 90 degrees. The maximum is one at theta=45 degrees; the two angle solutions for any shorter equal-height range merge here.
A different target height, wind, drag law, or launch constraint changes the optimum.

cards.title: Two angles for a target
items: For horizontal ground at distance R below the maximum, solve sin 2theta = Rg/v0². If 0<R<Rmax, there are generally two launch angles; at Rmax they merge.
No equal-height launch angle reaches a target beyond Rmax in the no-drag model.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Launch and landing elevations differ
subtitle: Use the full vertical quadratic; the range formula no longer applies.
takeaway: Pick the positive landing-time root, then multiply by horizontal velocity.

cards.title: Set the vertical target condition
items: Let launch height be y0 and target height be yf. Solve $yf-y0=v0 sintheta t - gt²/2$. Keep the positive root that corresponds to the physical landing event.
A negative or pre-launch root is not a flight time. A higher platform may have two crossings.

cards.title: Range to the target level
items: Once T is known, horizontal range from launch is $v0 costheta T$. If the projectile is launched from a height h above a level floor, use yf-y0=-h.
For theta=0 and h>0, this reduces to the horizontal-launch result.

cards.title: Height crossing can happen twice
items: A target elevation below the apex can be reached once on ascent and once on descent. The two roots have vertical velocities of opposite sign.
Root signs tell which branch intersects the specified height.

cards.title: Impact speed and angle
items: At impact, compute vx and vy separately, then speed and direction. For a lower landing level, impact speed exceeds launch speed in vacuum.
The squared-speed change is $-2g(y_f-y_0)$; it is independent of launch angle.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Projectiles on an inclined plane
subtitle: Resolve gravity along and normal to the slope; define launch angle from the slope.
takeaway: For an uphill slope alpha and launch angle beta above it, T = 2v0 sinbeta/(g cosalpha).

cards.title: Use slope-aligned coordinates
items: Let the plane rise at angle alpha. Choose s along the plane uphill and n perpendicular outward. Gravity components are downhill along s and into the plane along n.
The launch angle beta is measured above the incline; the horizontal angle is alpha+beta.

cards.title: Return to the same plane
items: Initial normal speed is v0 sinbeta. The normal coordinate returns to zero after a nonzero flight time. This time is finite for alpha below 90 degrees.
When alpha=0, recover ordinary ground-to-ground flight time for launch angle beta.

cards.title: Range along the incline
items: Along-plane displacement combines initial along-slope speed v0 cosbeta with downhill acceleration. Substitute T from the normal motion.
This formula describes a return to the same uphill plane and a valid forward landing.

cards.title: Optimize the slope range
items: At fixed launch speed and slope, maximize the product sinbeta cos(alpha+beta). The optimum measured from the horizontal is 45 degrees plus half the slope angle.
At alpha=0, the best launch is 45 degrees above horizontal.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Reachability and the safety envelope
subtitle: The envelope gives the highest point attainable at each horizontal coordinate for fixed speed.
takeaway: For launch from the origin in vacuum, the envelope is y = v0²/(2g) - gx²/(2v0²).

cards.title: Family of trajectories
items: At fixed speed v0, each launch angle gives a different parabola. For a fixed x, maximize y over launch angle; the boundary is the envelope of the family.
An envelope is not one projectile path; it is the boundary traced by the best angle at each x.

cards.title: Find the maximum y at fixed x
items: Set the derivative with respect to launch angle to zero. The maximizing slope obeys tantheta=v0²/(gx), for forward x>0.
As x approaches zero, the optimum approaches a vertical launch.

cards.title: Envelope equation and domain
items: Substitution gives the downward-opening safety parabola. For forward targets at or above launch level, a point below this boundary can be reached by some suitable angle before the projectile lands.
State the physical domain. The envelope does not make post-impact or underground portions of ideal parabolas physical.

cards.title: Read its intercepts
items: At x=0 the envelope height is the vertical-launch maximum. It meets y=0 at the maximum equal-height range. Dimensional and limit checks confirm the shape.
Increasing v0 raises and widens the envelope; increasing g lowers and narrows it.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Relative velocity in two dimensions
subtitle: Write the frame relation as a vector equation before resolving components.
takeaway: v_A/B = v_A - v_B; the relative vector points along how A moves as seen by B.

cards.title: Subtract vectors, not speeds
items: All velocities must be measured in a compatible frame. The velocity of A relative to B is the vector difference; the magnitude is found only after subtraction.
Subtracting speed magnitudes loses direction and fails for non-collinear motion.

cards.title: Use a velocity triangle
items: Draw v_B and v_A from a common origin; their difference is the vector from the tip of v_B to the tip of v_A. Label the reference frames on each velocity.
Frame chaining is additive; reverse a relation by reversing the vector.

cards.title: Rain and a moving observer
items: If rain falls vertically at speed vr and a person walks east at vm, rain relative to the person has a westward horizontal component. The apparent source lies forward of vertical.
If vm=3 and vr=4 m/s, the apparent direction is 36.9 degrees from vertical.

cards.title: Rate of separation in a plane
items: For relative position vector r and relative velocity vrel, the instantaneous rate of change of separation is the radial projection of vrel, not generally its full magnitude.
At zero initial separation, use the right-hand growth rate, which is |vrel|; the radial unit vector is undefined exactly at coincidence.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: River crossing: time, drift and aim
subtitle: Separate across-river and along-river components of the boat relative to ground.
takeaway: Crossing time depends on the across component; drift depends on the downstream component.

cards.title: Define current and boat velocity
items: Let +x point straight across, +y downstream. Boat velocity relative water plus water velocity relative ground gives the ground velocity.
If the boat points straight across, its across speed is vb and it drifts at current speed vr.

cards.title: Point straight across
items: For river width d and boat speed vb relative water, straight-across heading gives crossing time d/vb and drift vr times that duration.
This minimizes crossing time when the boat speed through water is fixed and the current is parallel to the bank.

cards.title: Land directly opposite
items: Aim upstream so the upstream component cancels the current. This is possible only if boat speed is at least the current speed.
The no-drift heading takes longer than pointing directly across. At vb=vr, crossing time diverges.

cards.title: Aim at a specified landing point
items: For any chosen heading, compute ground components first. Time is width divided by across component; drift is downstream component times that time.
Keep direction signs explicit: an upstream component is negative if downstream is positive.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Aircraft and wind
subtitle: The ground track is the vector sum of airspeed and wind velocity.
takeaway: Cancel crosswind with an opposite air-velocity component; compute ground speed from the along-track component.

cards.title: Start with the vector law
items: Airspeed is velocity relative to air; wind is air relative to ground. Their vector sum is the aircraft velocity over ground.
“Wind from west” means velocity toward east. Convert wind wording into a vector before choosing heading.

cards.title: Crosswind correction
items: For a desired due-north ground track and an eastward wind wx, the plane must point west of north so its west component cancels wx. The north component then sets ground speed.
A feasible heading requires |wx| no greater than the available airspeed.

cards.title: Wind with along-track component
items: Resolve wind into along-track and cross-track parts. Cancel the cross-track component; add the along-track wind to the remaining aircraft component.
A tailwind increases groundspeed; a headwind decreases it, while crosswind changes heading.

cards.title: Sign-audited example
items: A plane needs 200 km/h north over ground. Wind from west blows east at 40 km/h. The air velocity needs a 40 km/h west component and 200 km/h north component.
The heading is 11.31 degrees west of north, not east.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Angular motion and tangential speed
subtitle: Radians make arc length proportional to angle; angular rate converts to linear speed.
takeaway: For fixed radius, v = Romega; one full turn is 2π radians.

cards.title: Angular position and rate
items: Measure angle in radians. Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular position; its sign states rotation sense under the chosen convention. After a reversal, total angular path accumulates |dtheta|, not signed endpoint change.
One revolution is $2\pi$ rad, not 360 radians.

cards.title: Arc-length relation
items: For a circle of radius R, arc length is R times angle in radians. Differentiate to link tangential speed to angular speed.
Radians are dimensionless in SI, but retaining “rad” helps distinguish angular rate from ordinary frequency.

cards.title: Period and frequency
items: Period is time per revolution; frequency is revolutions per second. For steady rotation, angular speed magnitude equals 2πf; for nonuniform rotation, 2π/T is the cycle-averaged angular speed.
Do not use rpm directly in v=Romega; convert rpm to rad/s first.

cards.title: Quick conversion
items: For 120 rpm, divide by 60 to get 2 revolutions per second, then multiply by 2π. A rim of radius 0.5 m has tangential speed Romega and period 0.5 s. Its circumference is $2\pi r=\pi\ \mathrm{m}$, so two turns per second cover $2\pi\ \mathrm{m}$ each second.
Check units: m times s^-1 gives m/s.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Centripetal and tangential acceleration
subtitle: Velocity turns even when speed is constant; changing speed adds a tangential component.
takeaway: a = -Romega² rhat + Ralpha thetahat; inward magnitude is v²/R.

cards.title: Differentiate the rotating unit vectors
items: On a circle, position is R rhat. The radial unit vector rotates at angular speed omega, and the tangential unit vector rotates toward -rhat.
Acceleration contains a radial term because the direction of the velocity basis changes.

cards.title: Full circular acceleration
items: Differentiate the velocity vector: radius times angular speed in the tangential direction. The radial term points inward; the tangential term changes speed. Its sign follows angular acceleration under the chosen positive rotation sense.
At constant omega, only the inward component remains.

cards.title: Magnitudes and meanings
items: Tangential acceleration is the time rate of speed change; centripetal acceleration changes direction. They are perpendicular, so the total magnitude is their root-sum-square.
Centripetal acceleration is not a separate force; “centripetal force” is the net inward force in dynamics.

cards.title: Quick computation
items: At R=2 m and omega=3 rad/s, inward acceleration is 18 m/s². If angular acceleration is 4 rad/s², tangential acceleration is 8 m/s².
The acceleration vector points inward and along the tangent; it is not generally radial.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Curvature and the normal acceleration
subtitle: A curved path has an instantaneous osculating circle; normal acceleration sets its radius.
takeaway: rho = v² / |a_perp|. Tangential acceleration changes speed; normal acceleration changes direction.

cards.title: Resolve acceleration along velocity
items: At nonzero speed, decompose acceleration into a tangential component parallel to velocity and a normal component perpendicular to it.
a_t=\frac{dv}{dt},\qquad a_\perp=|\mathbf a-(\mathbf a\cdot\hat v)\hat v|
Only the perpendicular component bends the velocity direction.

cards.title: Radius of curvature
items: Over a short time, velocity direction turns by dphi while arc distance is ds=v dt. Curvature is dphi/ds; the normal acceleration is v² times curvature.
For a circle, rho is its ordinary radius and this becomes centripetal acceleration.

cards.title: Projectile at launch and apex
items: For gravity downward, at launch angle theta the normal component magnitude is g|costheta|. At the apex, velocity is horizontal so all g is normal.
For a vertical launch, the path is straight and rho is infinite; handle costheta=0 as a limit.

cards.title: Limits and interpretation
items: If normal acceleration vanishes at nonzero speed, the instantaneous path is straight and curvature is zero. At a zero-speed cusp, the usual velocity-based decomposition may fail.
A smaller rho means tighter turning for the same speed.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Kinematics method map and final checks
subtitle: Start from what is given, choose a model, then test signs and limiting cases.
takeaway: Name the frame, axis, interval, acceleration law and requested quantity before calculating.

cards.title: Route by the acceleration law
items: Constant a: use signed kinematic equations. Given a(t): integrate. Given a(v): separate dv/a(v). Given a(x): use v dv/dx. A graph may provide slopes or areas directly.
Use the simplest relation that matches the information; do not force every problem into one formula.

cards.title: Route projectile questions
items: Split x and y and share time. Equal elevations: use T, H and R formulas. Unequal elevations: solve the vertical quadratic. Incline: resolve along and normal to the plane.
Check the launch and landing levels before quoting the standard range.

cards.title: Route relative and circular questions
items: Relative motion: write frame-chaining vectors and define separation. Circular motion: keep tangential and normal acceleration separate. General path: use local curvature.
Relative velocity is a vector; a_c is acceleration, not force.

cards.title: Ten-second audit
items: Check units; sign convention; initial conditions; root time; distance versus displacement; model validity; and whether the path reaches the stated target before hitting another surface.
If an answer changes under relabelling the positive axis, a sign error is likely.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Variable laws: choose the independent variable
subtitle: The best integration variable is the one already present in the acceleration law.
takeaway: a(t), a(v), and a(x) lead to different first-order integrals; preserve branches and initial data.

cards.title: When acceleration is a function of time
items: Integrate the known function of time once for velocity and again for position. Each integration constant is fixed by a measured initial state.
Polynomial acceleration produces polynomial v and x; dimensions of every coefficient must match.

cards.title: When acceleration is a function of velocity
items: Separate the differential equation. Equilibria where a(v)=0 are approached asymptotically in many dissipative models; do not divide through an equilibrium without checking it.
A divergent time integral to an equilibrium signals asymptotic approach, not finite-time arrival.

cards.title: When acceleration is a function of position
items: Apply the chain rule and integrate between measured endpoints. The result is a speed-energy relation even when no energy model has been introduced.
Choose the sign of v from direction; v² alone cannot tell whether motion is forward or returning.

cards.title: Turning points and forbidden regions
items: A candidate trajectory can occupy only positions where the computed v² is non-negative. A zero of v may be a turn, a stopping point, or an asymptote depending on acceleration and time integral.
Check both the sign branch and the time to reach each endpoint.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Linear drag and terminal velocity
subtitle: A linear drag law is proportional to velocity relative to the surrounding medium.
takeaway: For downward-positive fall: v(t)=vT(1-e^(-t/tau)) from rest, with tau=m/b and vT=gtau.

cards.title: Set the sign convention
items: For a body moving vertically in still air, choose downward positive. Weight is +mg and linear drag is -bv. The equation is first-order and dissipative.
Drag opposes velocity relative to air; if the body rises, drag points downward too.

cards.title: Solve from rest
items: The equilibrium speed is the terminal speed. Subtract it from v to obtain an exponential decay equation for the speed difference. For times much shorter than the time constant, expansion gives velocity near gt and fall distance near half gt squared.
At t=0, v=0; as t grows, v approaches vT from below.

cards.title: Position and early-time limit
items: Integrating velocity gives the fall distance from rest. At short times the exponential expands to recover near-free-fall motion.
For t much smaller than tau, v is approximately gt; at long times position becomes nearly linear in time.

cards.title: Terminal speed is an equilibrium
items: At terminal speed, net acceleration is zero: drag balances weight. The velocity does not become exactly terminal at finite time in this model.
As b tends to zero, tau and vT grow and the finite-time solution tends to free fall.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Quadratic drag and terminal fall
subtitle: At larger Reynolds number, drag magnitude is often modelled proportional to speed squared.
takeaway: For downward-positive fall from rest: v=vT tanh(gt/vT), vT=sqrt(mg/k).

cards.title: State the quadratic law
items: For downward velocity v>=0, write drag magnitude kv² upward. The signed equation balances weight against drag; at v=0, drag vanishes and the initial acceleration is g.
For motion in either direction, the vector law is proportional to -v|v|, not always -v².

cards.title: Terminal speed
items: At equilibrium, mg=kvT². Dividing the differential equation by mg exposes a separable logistic-like form. Starting from rest, the terminal speed is approached asymptotically, not reached at finite time.
The terminal speed increases with mass and decreases with the square root of drag coefficient.

cards.title: Integrate from rest
items: Separate variables and integrate. The hyperbolic tangent satisfies the initial condition and approaches one at large argument.
At early time tanh zaboutz, giving vaboutgt; at late time v approaches vT.

cards.title: Do not confuse drag regimes
items: Linear and quadratic drag are idealisations whose use depends on Reynolds number, shape and flow. The coefficient k is not universal across objects or speeds.
A measured terminal speed can determine a drag parameter only after the force law and projected area are specified.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Stopping, reaction time and scaling
subtitle: A human response delay and a braking force are distinct stages.
takeaway: Reaction distance scales as v; constant-deceleration braking distance scales as v².

cards.title: Reaction phase
items: During a fixed reaction interval tr, speed is approximately unchanged. The vehicle travels forward before braking starts; this distance is already covered before the assumed braking acceleration acts.
At 20 m/s and 0.5 s, the reaction distance is 10 m.

cards.title: Braking phase
items: For constant deceleration magnitude b, use the no-time equation from initial speed v0 to rest. This is braking distance only.
The assumed b is constant and independent of speed; real tire-road limits may change the model.

cards.title: Combine and compare
items: Total distance is the sum of phases. Doubling speed doubles reaction distance but quadruples braking distance when the reaction time and b are fixed.
At high speed, braking distance dominates; at low speed, reaction distance can be a substantial fraction.

cards.title: Check a full example
items: For v0=20 m/s, tr=0.5 s and b=5 m/s², reaction distance is 10 m and braking distance 40 m; the total is 50 m. Substitution in $v^2=u^2-2bd=0$ checks the final speed at the end of braking.
Changing the assumed reaction time changes only the first term.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Projectile with linear drag
subtitle: For isotropic linear drag, horizontal and vertical ODEs decouple, but the landing event still matters.
takeaway: Solve x(t), y(t); find the positive ground-contact time from y(T)=0, then evaluate x(T).

cards.title: Equations in still air
items: With up positive, drag force is -b v as a vector. Let tau=m/b. Horizontal velocity decays exponentially; vertical velocity also has a terminal offset.
This model is isotropic and linear in velocity; it is not the standard quadratic high-speed drag law.

cards.title: Integrate the components
items: For launch components v0x and v0y from the origin, integrate each velocity with x(0)=y(0)=0. Horizontal position approaches tauv0x as tto∞ even though landing generally occurs earlier.

cards.title: Find the actual landing time
items: Landing at the launch elevation requires the positive nonzero root of y(T)=0. In general this transcendental equation is solved numerically; use the root consistent with the descending branch.
The integral of vx to infinite time is not the projectile range; the projectile has already landed.

cards.title: Then evaluate range and limits
items: The horizontal range is x(T). As b tends to zero, the equations tend to the vacuum trajectory and the landing time tends to 2v0y/g.
A correct range calculation must use one common finite T for both coordinates.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Constant horizontal deceleration
subtitle: A deliberately simple headwind model adds a constant horizontal acceleration.
takeaway: Vertical motion fixes T; horizontal displacement includes the acceleration term.

cards.title: Separate the components
items: Assume a constant horizontal acceleration -aw throughout flight and no vertical drag. Then vertical motion is unchanged, so equal-height flight time is still set by v0y and g.
A real aerodynamic headwind generally gives a speed-dependent force, not a constant deceleration.

cards.title: Range correction
items: At the equal-height landing time T=2v0y/g, evaluate x(T). The change from vacuum range is half aw T squared; aw is a positive deceleration magnitude opposing the initial horizontal motion.
As aw tends to zero, recover the vacuum range.

cards.title: Forward landing condition
items: A positive horizontal acceleration is not implied; if deceleration is strong enough, horizontal velocity can reverse before landing and x(T) may be zero or negative.
Distinguish signed horizontal displacement from path length when the projectile reverses horizontally.

cards.title: Angle dependence
items: For fixed launch speed, a steeper angle increases flight time and therefore increases the correction aw T²/2 in this model. The optimum launch angle is no longer generally 45 degrees.
This expression has dimensions of length and vanishes at zero flight time.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Interception with gravity: solve at a common time
subtitle: A moving target and projectile must occupy the same position at one shared time.
takeaway: For fixed launch speed, impose the target position equation on the projectile trajectory and solve for positive t.

cards.title: Write both position laws
items: Let the target begin at r0 and move at constant velocity vt. The projectile starts at the origin with unknown launch vector v0 and acceleration gvec.
\mathbf r_p=\mathbf v_0t+\tfrac12\mathbf g t^2,\quad\mathbf r_T=\mathbf r_0+\mathbf v_Tt
Do not treat the target as stationary in the projectile frame unless the frame transformation is applied to both velocity and acceleration.

cards.title: Impose interception
items: Set positions equal and solve for the required launch vector as a function of candidate time. Fixed launch speed imposes one scalar equation.
Each positive solution time gives a candidate launch direction; reject candidates that hit the ground or an obstacle first.

cards.title: Fixed-speed condition
items: For prescribed v0 magnitude, solve the squared magnitude equation. Gravity makes this generally a quartic in t; there may be zero, one, or several physical solutions.
A no-gravity interception reduces to a quadratic condition in 1/t after choosing the frame.

cards.title: Physical root audit
items: Check t>0, the initial and target positions, velocity direction, and whether the target is actually reachable under the model. Root counting is part of the solution.
“Aim directly at the target’s current position” is generally wrong when the target moves or gravity acts.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Coriolis deflection: first-order estimate
subtitle: In a rotating Earth frame, horizontal motion acquires a small sideways acceleration.
takeaway: For northward speed v at latitude lambda, eastward Coriolis acceleration is about 2Omegav sinlambda in the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.title: Rotating-frame acceleration
items: In a frame rotating with angular velocity Omega, the Coriolis term is -2 Omega cross v. It is perpendicular to velocity and changes direction, not speed, to first order.
This is an apparent acceleration in the rotating frame, not a new interaction force in an inertial frame.

cards.title: Local northward motion
items: Resolve Earth rotation into local north and vertical components. For horizontal northward motion at latitude lambda, the horizontal Coriolis acceleration points east in the Northern Hemisphere.
At the equator, this horizontal component vanishes for purely northward motion.

cards.title: Estimate sideways displacement
items: If the northward speed and flight time T are nearly constant, treat the small eastward acceleration as constant over the interval.
This first-order estimate neglects feedback of the sideways velocity into Coriolis acceleration.

cards.title: Numerical scale
items: At latitude 45 degrees, with vN=500 m/s and T=20 s, the estimate is about 10.3 m east. Use actual flight time from vertical motion, not range divided by speed unless the geometry warrants it.
The deflection scales linearly with Omega, vN, and sinlambda, and quadratically with time.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Planar pursuit: specify geometry before solving
subtitle: A pursuit problem is a coupled ODE, not a universal power-law curve.
takeaway: With target at (vt t,0) and pursuer initially at (0,d), derive the line-of-sight ODE before seeking a path.

cards.title: State the setup explicitly
items: Let the target start at the origin and move along +x at constant speed vt. A pursuer starts at (0,d), has constant speed vp, and always aims at the target’s current position.
Changing the initial geometry changes the path; no single pursuit curve applies to every setup.

cards.title: Write the pursuit equations
items: Let dx and dy be the pursuer coordinates, and D the instantaneous distance to target. Its velocity is vp times the unit vector toward the target.

cards.title: Use relative range for capture
items: For target-minus-pursuer separation vector r, its radial rate is at most vt-vp. If vp>vt, the separation decreases at a rate bounded away from zero, so capture occurs in finite time.
The bound gives capture time no greater than initial separation divided by vp-vt.

cards.title: Solve the path with the stated data
items: The ODE generally requires numerical integration for the trajectory and capture time. At each step update target position and point the pursuer along the current line of sight.
A claimed closed form must satisfy the ODE and the initial conditions; checking only dimensions is not enough.

source: Reference: kinematics-1d/Kinematics-1d.md and motion-in-two-dimensions/Motion-in-two-dimensions.md; equations independently checked

title: Model limits: Newtonian, vacuum and smooth paths
subtitle: A correct formula includes the regime in which it is meaningful.
takeaway: Use Newtonian kinematics for v much less than c; distinguish model assumptions from algebraic identities.

cards.title: Newtonian speed boundary
items: At high speed, relativistic momentum is gammamv rather than mv. The fractional correction is approximately v²/(2c²) when v is small compared with c.
A 1 percent momentum correction begins near vabout0.14c.

cards.title: Separate identity from model
items: The chain rule identity a=v dv/dx is kinematic. Constant acceleration, uniform gravity, vacuum projectile motion, and a chosen drag law are additional model assumptions.
A derivation can be algebraically correct and still use the wrong physical model.

cards.title: Check low and high limits
items: Remove a small effect by taking its parameter to zero: drag coefficient to zero, wind speed to zero, or Earth rotation Omega to zero. The result should reduce to the simpler model.
Do not extrapolate a low-speed drag law or constant-acceleration approximation beyond its regime.

cards.title: State domain and event
items: A trajectory formula describes motion only until the first physical constraint or contact event. Roots need positive time, and a path after impact is not part of the same free-flight phase.
t\geq0,\qquad\text{stop the model at first contact}
Before reporting a range, identify which surface is hit and at what time.
